utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Oric, good afternoon to you. Can you follow the proceedings in a language you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. Yes, I can follow the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, and good afternoon to members of the Defence team. My name is Jan Wubben, senior trial attorney, lead counsel for the Prosecution team, together with counsel Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink. And I ask for allowance of special legal assistant at our desk to sit down, Mr. Marc Ellenbogen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is with pleasure that we say yes. Anyone who is young and wants to learn will always get the support of the Tribunal. Yes, appearances for Mr. Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon also to my colleagues from the OTP. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, together with Mr. John Jones, appearing here for Mr. Naser Oric. Joining us here today are also our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, as well as our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let me start with some preliminaries myself. First of all, I should like to inform you, or confirm to you if you are informed already, that earlier on in the day, we handed down a decision, a written decision, on the Defence's urgent motion regarding late disclosure of evidence and to recall a witness, which motion was filed on the 18th of this -- November. As you may or may not know, we granted the motion. And on that score, I would enjoin the Prosecution to start the ball rolling to bring back Mr. Eric to continue with his testimony. That's number one. Number two is we have pending the Prosecution confidential motion for the admission of written statements of witnesses, pursuant to Rule 92 bis (C), which was filed on the 27th of September, 2004. I am about, on behalf of the Trial Chamber, to pronounce an oral decision on this motion. Just for the record, I just want to remind that you the Trial Chamber has already ruled on this motion in relation to one of the persons mentioned therein, that is, Mr. Bogdanovic, while the request regarding the other person, Ms. Bozic, was withdrawn by the Prosecution. So the only person that remains to be dealt with is Mr. Bogdanovic. Before proceeding with the oral decision, I would point out to you that while going through the documents, relevant documents, I noticed that there is, as yet, no official translation of the medical report of Dr. Ljubovic. If there is no objection forthcoming on the -- by -- on the part of the Defence, in other words, if you accept the summary that we were provided with the last -- one of the last sittings, then I will proceed with the oral decision. If not, obviously, we will have to postpone it. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. So basically at this point, I would like to give an oral decision. The Trial Chamber is now pronouncing itself on the admission -- on the request by the Prosecution for the admission into evidence of the written statement of Miladin Bogdanovic, pursuant to Rule 92 bis (C) of our Rules. For the record, it's to be noted that on the 27th of September, 2004, the Prosecution filed a confidential motion for the admission of written statements of three witnesses, including that of Miladin Bogdanovic, pursuant to 92 bis (C) on the basis that he had been incapacitated by a stroke. On 30th September 2004, the Prosecution filed a motion and contended that the medical report by the Prosecution to establish that this witness was, by reason of bodily or mental condition, unable to testify orally, had not been translated, and that the interpretation provided by the Prosecution was incorrect. However, in its response, the Defence did not challenge the admission into evidence the witness statement on the basis that the other requirements of Rule 92 bis were all fulfilled. Following an exchange of correspondence and communications between the parties, as well as upon the suggestion the Trial Chamber, the appointment of a medical expert, Dr. Senadin Ljubovic was agreed upon. Mr. Ljubovic conducted his examination on the 19th of November of this year, and concluded that Miladin Bogdanovic was not fit to give testimony in a trial and answer questions pertaining to events which occurred more than 10 years ago. The Trial Chamber is, therefore, satisfied on a balance of probabilities that Miladin Bogdanovic is unable to testify orally before the Tribunal by reason of his bodily and/or mental condition. The Trial Chamber is further satisfied that the subject matter of the statement of Miladin Bogdanovic, namely evidence relating to Jezestica prior to its attack on the 8th of August, 1992, and also on the 7th and 9th of January of the following year, 1993, is relevant pursuant -- is relevant to this case, pursuant to Rule 89(C). Finally, the Trial Chamber additionally considers that the statement of Bogdanovic goes to prove matter other than the acts and conduct of the accused as charged in the indictment. The Trial Chamber further considers that the ultimate probative value of the statement of Miladin Bogdanovic shall be assessed in the light of any existing evidence of cumulative nature, and with, obviously, due consideration to the fact that the Defence cannot cross-examine the evidence contained in the witness statement. For the reasons set out above, but also for the non-objection on the part of the trial -- of the Defence, the Trial Chamber grants the Prosecution motion and admits the written statement of Miladin Bogdanovic into evidence, pursuant to Rule 92 bis (C). And that settles the matter. There is another matter that was -- my attention was drawn to immediately after the sitting, when Ms. Trifunovic gave evidence, and that is that at a certain point in time, we were confronting the witness her two statements: the one which was tendered into evidence by the Defence, I think it's marked D81 or 82; and the statement to the Prosecution, which goes back to 2001, I think, or 2003. The problem that I see is the following: That I don't think it helps at all the Trial Chamber to maintain a situation whereby the statement given to the Republika Srpska authorities is tendered and received in evidence, while the statement tendered or given to the Prosecution, which also contains her signature on which she was asked questions, is not tendered in evidence. So our suggestion is, unless you have got an objection, either yourselves or on the part of the Defence, to tender that document also in evidence. But - I'm making it very clear - only insofar as it relates to the signature of that witness. In other words, the document itself, the statement itself, will not in any way be used by the Trial Chamber in substitution of the oral testimony that she gave here. All right? Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no objection. We will comply with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So that will be tendered in evidence with this caveat ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That will be P?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: P, because it was tendered by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number will be P418.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. MR. DI FAZIO: Do you actually have a physical copy of the statement? Otherwise, we'll undertake to provide one to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have. Each one of us has a copy of that statement. MR. DI FAZIO: If there's any problem with the registrar not having a copy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, you can liaise with my secretary. Mr. Registrar, have my copy. It's not marked or anything. Do you have a copy yourself? Okay. We will have that admitted here. Show it -- make sure that you show it to the Defence so that they are fully aware of which document we're talking about. So before I give you the floor, I was informed this morning by my senior legal officer, Mr. von Hebel, that he had in turn been informed that you may have a problem with this witness, and that she has forgotten her reading glasses. I think the problem goes beyond not having reading glasses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is no problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: There had been a problem that she has, indeed, forgotten her glasses. I notified Defence counsel of it this morning and requested the Victims and Witness Unit to address with support. The Victims and Witness Unit confirmed that they have recently been able to solve the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's good. All right. Do you have any preliminaries, preliminary matters to raise? Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: It's not a big issue, it's a matter of professionalism, Your Honour. Yesterday evening, we received a list of exhibits, together with the ERN numbers, two of them without ERN numbers. And this afternoon, at around 1.00, I received an additional list without any notifying in advance, and I regret that it hadn't been announced that, all of a sudden, they send an additional list, just one or two hours in advance of the start of the trial. And that is not according to the practice of this Trial Chamber and the ruling in that regard. I regret that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as for professional standards, I will put it like this: Yesterday we spent the whole day with the OTP's case manager discussing the fact that we had the documents and that we would be forwarding a list of documents, including the ERN numbers. We pointed out, however, that it was essential for us to get the proofing notes in order to be able to put together a complete document. We then agreed to forward a provisional list, which is what we did. Everything that we had received by 6.30 yesterday afternoon, including the proofing notes, we have since forwarded. Once we received the proofing notes, we saw that there were facts in it that required further examination on our part. We were put in a situation where we had to study the documents and work on their translations through the whole night. By the time we got back to the OTP, we had done whatever we could. One thing we have to understand is I have two assistants here working with me. My office is back in Sarajevo, and that is also where all of our documents are. I asked the OTP yesterday that such information be forwarded in a timely fashion in the future, because that very much conditions the kind of response that we can give. May it be understood that we have few assistants working with us, we have limited resources at our disposal, and I believe we have done the best we could. We have all spent a sleepless night to get this list ready; therefore, there can be no talk of professional standards here. Please try to understand my submission in this light.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not our intention, for sure, to escalate this into a major argument. Our recommendation is to try and cooperate with one another as much as you can so as to avoid these incidents being repeated. They are not conducive to the good environment, good and healthy environment that I spoke of in the very first day of this trial. There being nothing else, no further business to transact, let's -- yes. Usher, you can bring the witness in, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I want to make sure that what I am saying in English is being interpreted to you in your own language. Are you receiving interpretation in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are about to give evidence in this trial against Naser Oric. Our Rules require that before you start giving evidence, you make a solemn declaration that, in the course of your testimony, you will be saying the truth, speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. I am going to read out the statement bit by bit, and I would like you to repeat this statement as soon and as you receive it from the interpreters. I'm going to start now. I, Slavka Matic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I, Slavka Matic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That I will speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That I will speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The whole truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The whole truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam, you can sit down. I would like to welcome you to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am the presiding judge. My name is Carmel Agius, and I come from the island of Malta. To my right I have Judge Hans Hendrik Brydensholt, from Denmark, and to my left I have Judge Albin Eser from Germany. Together we form the Trial Chamber. And on above of the Trial Chamber, once more I welcome you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The procedure we follow is a simple one. The Prosecution, I think it will be Mr. Wubben, will start questioning you, and when he finishes with his series of questions, you will then be cross-examined by a member of the Defence team, which will be Madam Vidovic. Your obligation and your duty and responsibility in terms of the solemn declaration that you have made with us is that, in answering these questions, you will do your utmost to be truthful and complete in your answers without making a distinction as to who is putting the question to you. You have no right to discriminate, for example, in favour of the Prosecution, who has summoned you as its witness here, or discriminate against the Defence because you think you shouldn't testify in their favour. So basically your duty is to answer all questions truthfully and fully. Did I make myself understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If at any time during your testimony you need you break, you feel tired, or you need some assistance, please draw my attention and we'll come forward and assist you immediately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honours, there's one preliminary matter, which is that we don't understand this witness to be illiterate. On the contrary, she's signed statements and has apparently attended elementary school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am informed that she is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We would contest that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I didn't want to raise the matter. But once you have raised the matter, I will raise it with her. But I am informed that she is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If it could be clarified with her, and it's a matter we may raise in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Matic, can you read and write?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I can't, because I was out of school in 1954. That was a long time ago. I lived in the country; therefore, I no longer pursued such activities. All I know is sometimes I can read some letters and I can sign things. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you know how to sign your name, but you don't know how to read or write.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last name, yes, I can read it. I know the exact sequence of letters in my last name. If someone else puts their signature there, this is not something that I can read. I can only read my own last name. As for everything else, I really don't know much about it, because I've never really had any need for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Are you happy with that, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's a matter we may need to cross-examine her upon. For the moment, we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's the situation as it was related to me before we started this sitting. So, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Wubben:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Slavka Matic.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will put forward questions to you related to the case you're about to testify. My first questions will focus on your personal background, and please answer with yes or no. Is your name Slavka Matic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you born on the 13th of October, 1944?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you of Serb ethnic origin?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is your occupation, your current occupation, a housewife?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes. Nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me go back with you to the events in 1992. That's 12 years ago from now on. Where did you live in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: In the village of Bjelice, Bjelovac municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Bjelovac municipality in the municipality of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes. Bratunac municipality is our main municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You live there with your family?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You live there in your own house?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes. I built a house in 1967.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you live there with your husband and two daughters?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me the name of your daughters?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Snezana Matic, born in 1965; that's my elder daughter. Gordana is the younger; she was born in 1967.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the name of your husband?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Radivoje Matic. His father's name was Ilija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you lived in Bjelovac, and Bjelovac had also surrounding hamlets.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes. My husband lived in Sikiric. My married name was Sikiric. For four years I lived there. And after that, for four years, in 1967, I built a house in Bjelovac. I just crossed the river.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Bjelovac a Serbian city, a Serb-originated city, with a majority of Serbs in it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the hamlet you talked about, the hamlet of Sikiric, is that also a Serb hamlet?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Down there, as far as the places near Drina go, the majority population is Serb. But uphill there's a hamlet, Lanista Skela, these are populated by Muslims. There were no Serbs there. That's a place called Skela, near Sikirici, very close to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in 1992, there had been an attack upon your village. Can you tell us of the date of that attack?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: The 14th of December.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that, to be precise, the 14th of December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to that attack, were there tensions between regions in -- as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: There were tensions, yes, as the Muslims had left earlier on to the villages where the majority population was Muslim. And they fired shots nearly every day, so you couldn't move freely in your fields. So we worked just a little bit and then withdrew into shelters. And that's how we lived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had there been a kind of organising between villages or within villages or hamlets to a kind of army or a kind of defence or village guard, or none, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: There was a village guard organised in our village. They stood guard by night, securing the village, protecting it somehow. I wasn't there. From time to time, they went to stand guard. That was the village guard. There was no other guard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that village guard, that consisted of civilians or also soldiers, like Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Only civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did it --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: We didn't have any sort of army. The men were simply civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they wear any uniforms, these civilians?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: As far as I was able to see, I didn't see anyone in uniform. It may be that somebody had a uniform, but I didn't go there. I stayed at home with my children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they have any arms, this village guard?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, some may have had a hunting rifle from before; some had a pistol; some may have been reserve policemen. Or maybe they bought a weapon, I don't know. I can't know for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To what extent were these village guards organised? I mean, had they been trained as a village guard? Did they exercise? Or can you tell us something about that, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. I can't say. My husband didn't participate in that sort of organisation. They simply called upon him in the evenings, when it was his turn to stand guard and protect the village. I don't know anything else about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Standing guard to protect the village, what does that mean? Can you tell us something about it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Well, what do I know? I don't know why this had to be done. I didn't know. I was surprised. I wondered what was going on and why.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question now: Your husband, he participated in this village guard. Did he have any arms, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: He didn't bring any weapons home. I don't remember seeing any weapons. My children were scared of weapons, and I wouldn't have allowed him to bring weapons into the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, to be complete, my question is: Did your children, your daughters, also participate in the village guard?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: No. No. At home -- they were at home in the evenings together with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you also confirm that there were not any weapons in the family house at the time of the attack, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I know, there were no weapons, and there couldn't have been any weapons in the house without my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you told the Judges the day of the attack was the 14th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time did this attack start?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I don't know exactly. I know that I got up at around 6.00, or a quarter past 6.00, and as I said, I was standing in for a woman in the direction of the school. It was still dark when the attack started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You went in the direction of the school. Why did you -- did you have a job in the school? What did you do over there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: I was standing in for a woman who asked me to clean the school because she was ill, and that morning I went there. I had done that on a few previous occasions, in the morning. On that day that woman was killed, that's when the misfortune happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Another question about your job. Was cleaning the school the only activity you participated in at the school?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes. I never participated in anything else, anywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I mean a job, an activity in the school, did you only clean the school, or did you also do another activity at the school?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Later on, they brought things to the school, and I was there only from time to time. There were other women there who did that. They were distributing food for the village guards, because nobody was employed anywhere, nobody had work. So we had to eat, and somebody brought food in from Bratunac. But who it was, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, about the starting date and time of the attack in question, so you went to that school with a view to do cleaning activities over there; is that true?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened? How come you noticed that there was an attack going on?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: I set out in the direction of the school. It's about one kilometre, or 750 metres from my house to the school. When I was halfway to the school, shooting started from all sides. I didn't know what was going on, who was firing. I saw a man come out of a yard. I just saw the man walking in front of me. It was still dark. I recognised him and I called him by name. His name was Petko Dzokanovic. I said, What's this, Petko, is it an attack? And then he said, Well, it looks like it is. And then I wondered what to do. I didn't know whether I should go home or continue on my way. But I thought it wasn't anything really dangerous, and so I went on to the school. When I reached the school, there were bullets firing at the school, the home, and there was a woman, as I said, at the school, her name was Nikolija Todorovic, and I said to her, Turn the lights out, and I she. She asked me what was going on, and I said there was an attack. And she said, What kind of attack? And I said, I don't know. Then I went to my nephew, Milisav, who lived 15 or 20 metres away from the school. I rang the bell and he came out and he said, What's going on, aunt? And I said to him, There's shooting from all sides. It looks like the Muslims are attacking us. And he was surprised. He ran out of the house. I went back to the school, and when I got there, I saw my brother Ilija, who was on his way towards the river Drina. I asked him where he was going, and he said he was going to accompany his son Milisav, because Cvetko had been wounded and they were going to take him there. I stayed there for awhile, and then my sister-in-law Sveta arrived. She was crying and shouting, They've killed Milisav and my son Stojan. In fact, Stojan survived but Milisav died. Stojan was only wounded. When I heard what had happened and that we were surrounded, and when I learned what was going on at the river Drina, I started going home. I couldn't get through. I followed the canal. I crawled, I crouched down, until I arrived at the house of Cvetko Lukic. And there I saw a man in front of Cvetko's house. There was a terrace there, and he was wounded --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. Thank you, witness. So you decided to go back, you decided to go back to your house, or did you go in another direction?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: I decided to go home, but I made a detour, because Cvetko's house and my house are about 300 metres apart, so I passed by Cvetko's house, intending to go back towards my own house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. My question is, then: What did you see at or near Cvetko's house? And what is the family name of Cvetko?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Lukic. Cvetko Lukic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what did you notice there? What did you see upon arriving?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: I saw a man, as I said, who had been wounded. There was a rifle next to him; that was his rifle. Borka arrived. She raised her hand to show the direction from which they were shooting, and they wounded her. I don't remember whether it was her right arm or the left. But I retreated to the canal quickly, because Cvetko's house is some 15 metres away from the canal. I crawled back --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, witness, I need to ask you to pay attention to the fact that I put forward a question to you, and please don't go too extensively in all the issues related to that question.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is: You noticed a person who had been wounded at Cvetko Lukic's house, and that there was a rifle. Can you tell something about that rifle, or did there happen anything to that rifle?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: It stayed there. It was probably his, because he was guarding the waterworks. But I don't know his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you notice where the shooting came from related to that attack?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: I noticed that it came from the direction of the school towards my house. On the right-hand side, there's a stream there, a creek, and from there, there was heavy shooting. And I retreated to some blocks. There was a woman standing there. She asked me where I was going, and I said I wanted to go home in order to see what was happening to my family. And she replied, You can't pass through. At Nikola's house, look there. So I looked there, and Nikola's house was on fire. And there were two men standing at one corner and two on the other. I couldn't recognise them --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, witness, again, one moment, please. My question was: Did you notice any attackers? Now, do I see it correctly that at that time, when you left the house where you saw the wounded person with the rifle, that you at that time didn't see any persons you linked to the attack?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw two at Nikola's house. That's what I said. I saw two at Nikola's house, with yellow ribbons on their heads. It wasn't our men, it wasn't Serbs. It was the Muslims, it was their army, Naser Oric's army. Who else would it belong to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One moment, witness. Can you tell me more about those two persons you saw? Were these persons soldiers, these persons with yellow ribbons on their heads, or other --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: They had weapons in their hands; they had backpacks on their backs. They were probably soldiers. They had rifles. It was very dark, really, and I couldn't really see their clothes very well. The fog was very thick. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you noticed, indeed, that there were ribbons on their forehead?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you noticed the colour of that ribbon?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: I think it was yellow. That's what I thought it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you noticed also whether or not they wore uniforms or typical clothes?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, their clothes were grey, but I couldn't make out whether it was a camouflage kind of clothing. It seemed to be military, the kind of clothing that individuals wore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did you think these were Muslims, that it was their army?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: I didn't think, I knew exactly. Because Nikola's house was on fire. It wouldn't have been Serbs that would have set fire to Nikola's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know that these Muslims, armed men, set fire on Nikola's house?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Who else would it have been? I heard across the stream, on my right-hand side, in the direction of my house, Berzadic Hajrudin yelling out, Surrender Chetniks, we'll catch you all alive. I heard him well. I understood what he was saying. I recognised his voice because he was a neighbour of mine. He lived a little way away from my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please spell out the name of that person that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Berzadic Hajrudin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how do you know a person like that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Well, we used to socialise for quite a long time. We were delegates in the local commune, so we knew each other quite well. We would have conversations. We would chat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you recognise him? Was it his face, his --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: By his voice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Wubben, sorry to interrupt you. We need to clear it now. Did she say Hajrudin Berzadic or Berzadic?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please answer that question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Berzadic or Begzadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Berzadic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Berzadic, okay. Yes, Mr. Wubben, please. Sorry to interrupt you, but I think it was important at this stage, because we avoided three or more questions on that, like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you recall after, it's now 12 years, what this person was yelling?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you expect her not to, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, let me tell you, these big tragedies that happened, they're hard to forget, although later on there is trauma. But a lot of time has gone by, and during that time I would recall the names, the attack. I've lived there for 41 years. I knew people of both ethnic groups; I knew them well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you recognise other persons being -- participating in the attack by this Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: I couldn't recognise them because they were 40 or 50 metres away from me. But let me tell you, it was quite dark. It was foggy, very foggy. I saw a few small groups of people, but I couldn't recognise any of them, so I wouldn't be able to tell you their names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you, indeed, confirmed that it was the army of Naser Oric. What did you make to think that or to conclude that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I wonder if Mr. Wubben means affirmed. "Confirmed," I don't know what the witness is confirming. It's a small point, but we certainly don't want it to be suggested that she's confirming some other statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will rephrase the question myself for you, Mr. Wubben, if you don't mind. Earlier on you mentioned Naser's army, Naser Oric's army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How can you be so sure about that, and how do you know about Naser Oric's army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think anything else but that he was in command, he commanded it. Although I haven't stated that previously, sometimes from the woods above our village, they would threaten us, only we didn't believe them. They would say that their commander, Naser Oric, would arrive on a white horse. I didn't believe it until it all happened. And there was a young man called Slobodan Petrovic who was taken prisoner; he was 16 or 17 years old, I can't be sure. And after there was an exchange, there was some sort of an exchange, and he was exchanged, and he told us that he had seen a Naser Oric there. And that was the name that they used to refer to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But you didn't see Naser Oric himself on the day of the attack, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, never. I didn't even know him. I didn't see him on that day. I don't want to do anything -- to say anything wrong, but I don't know, maybe somebody else can prove this, but I can't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, madam. Mr. Wubben, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This story about the Naser Oric army and Naser Oric in command, who did inform you of that? Was that friends, neighbours, or perhaps this Petrovic Slobodan, or someone else?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: That young man who lived across from my house, he had a brother. And when their village was burnt, he came and he was with us, until he was killed. He was killed in the attack, that young man, Slobodan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue. Did he inform you, or someone else?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Well, stories went around, and it was he who informed us mostly. But otherwise it was others as well. But I don't know where they got the information. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's not waste more time on this, Mr. Wubben, because I imagine both you and Madam Vidovic know that whether Oric was the commander or not will not result from the testimony of witnesses like the one we have now but from other sources, if at all. So let's proceed to something else, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also notice, when you saw these groups of attackers, that there was a kind of communication between those men, those attackers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can ask a direct question; I would allow it. Did you hear them communicating with each other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't hear them. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were a witness of something you considered as an attack. Who, as you did notice, who did the attackers fight against? Where did they shoot at? Did they shoot at people, at the houses? Can you tell us something about what you saw and heard?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: They shot at everything, at whatever they could. Let me tell you, that day - I find this very difficult - 68 people were killed in my area. They killed my two daughters at my doorstep, and they killed my husband, too. I found out on that very day about my two daughters having been killed, and my husband, too. I saw the body of my husband, I identified it, but not my daughters because they were outside the house and I was not able to reach them. I saw Bozo with my own eyes. He had been killed in his summer kitchen. He was lying on his back. I also saw Milun Ilic. He was right behind my house. I was not able to identify his body, but I did the next day, at 1500 hours, when we collected the bodies. I also saw Radovan Vucetic --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. I would like to proceed by taking you back in time, starting from that place, that house of Cvetko Lukic. From there you proceed on -- going in the direction of your house, and there you learned whatever was this person identified by you, shouting. What did you come across? Did you see there any attackers? Were they shooting, and who were they attacking, if so?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Well, I told you who they were attacking. Of course they were shooting. I couldn't get out of the ditch. Whenever they saw someone, they would shoot at them, no matter who. Whether it was a man or a woman. Whoever tried to cross the street was shot at, that's who they were attacking. I didn't precisely ask them why they were there, what they were doing, or whom they were attacking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what was the response by the villagers? Was there any response, if so, and meaning was there any defence of the village or the area against this attack?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, I never saw one of our men shoot back. There were sounds of rifles being fired, but that was a river valley; there's the river to the left of my house and the woods to the right. I can't really say who was doing the shooting. There was sounds of shooting resonating. I only saw that man next to Cvetko's house. He had been wounded. I don't know what his name was, but I know that he was the keeper of the waterworks. On my way back home, way back from Cvetko's house, that was what I saw. As for those of our men who had survived, I thought that they had all been killed. That's what I thought at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also witness that attackers were shooting at men, women, whatever, who were on the field or somewhere?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Well, like I said a while ago, whoever left their homes didn't make it. They would just turn their rifles on them and shoot them. There is a borderline near the Drina river. That's where they were. There's a huge borderline running between the two fields. And whoever they saw crossing the road or moving about, they killed them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice that there had been goods taken out of the houses, if so?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: I was not able to see that, because mainly, on that day, they were torching things. When they reached the houses, maybe they would enter some of the houses, but this is not something that I was able to see. I only saw smoke rising from the houses. Because I was in a column, I couldn't see them take anything out of the houses. I wasn't near enough to see it. I only saw the smoke rising from the burning houses, but I didn't see the people who were actually doing the looting, although I bet there were some of those there, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll come back to that issue later. But you also stated that they were torching houses or things. What do you mean by that? What did you make -- what makes you think that they were making -- they were burning or whatever?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not that I thought something. I only saw smoke rising from those houses who I was familiar with, and I knew who the houses belonged to. This is something I saw with my own eyes. I can't tell you who was doing the torching, but it certainly wasn't the Serbs. That's all I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was it certain that it wasn't the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: On that day, the Serbs were defending rather than attacking each other. They stood up to defend their village, and that's why so many of them were killed. There weren't sufficient people there to put up an adequate defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you actually see houses burning in the hamlet of Sikiric at the time of the attack?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did. That could have been sometime about -- I can't give you the exact time. It may have been at 9.00 or 10.00. Smoke descended over the whole village of Sikirici. This is something that I'm certain about because I saw it with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you know the hamlet of Sikiric well?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Of course I do. I spent four years there; I lived there with my husband. As I said, back in 1967, I built a house in Bjelovac, or in 1966. But in 1963, I got married in Sikirici and lived there. I knew all of the inhabitants. My husband's family lived there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've already confirmed that, but can you, because of that knowledge, also identify the houses that were burning at the time of the attack?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to give us the names of the people or the family who owned those houses that were burning at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please tell us those names, and please be specific and not too quick in pronouncing the name.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: The houses that were torched: Desimir Matic, my husband's brother; Mirko Matic; Vidoje Ilic. Let me think. Ljubisav Nedeljkovic, Ratko Nedeljkovic. They were both killed on that day, Ljubica and Ratko, Ratko's son. Ljubica's sister, Jevrenja [phoen]. They were all aged over 60. Nedeljkovic, let me think. Mladen Nedeljkovic. Milomir was also killed on that day. All of their houses were ablaze. I remember that well. Milomir Tanasic, who was also killed on that day too, and his house too was on fire. Grozda Simic was also killed on that day, and her house burned down. Zlatan Simic was killed; that's Grozda's son, also on that same day. And that's when all of these things burned down and all these people were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you give you another thought to take your time to recollect and recall your memory of the houses burning in Sikiric, can you come up with other names as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can help her, Mr. Wubben, please.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Should I continue with the houses that were burning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please, the houses in Sikiric.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Well, in Sikiric, there's also something that I forgot about. Pero Petrovic, or Petar, whatever his name is, but I know the man well, his house too was ablaze. All the houses in Sikiric had been torched, all the Serb houses. The Muslim houses still stand; they were never set alight. There are people living there, whether refugees or whoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you noticed that all the houses were torched except for the houses belonging to the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And including all those houses that were burning -- excuse me, witness, I will put forward the question to you, and then repeat. Including all those houses that were burned, was there also the house of a family called Tanasic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the full name of that --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Milomir Tanasic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a family name like Mitrovic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give me the full name? And if there are more houses with same family name, can you specify also?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Milomir Tanasic; Mitrovic Rado; Mitrovic Cvetko, all of them killed on that day. Mitrovic Veso, he's still alive; he wasn't killed. Mitrovic Miko, that's what his name was. But I'm not sure what his real name was, but his last name was Mitrovic and we called him Miko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there also a house of Mitrovic, with full name Veselin?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's two adjacent houses. There were three brothers. They had houses that were adjacent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a house belonging to a family with the name Rankic? And if so, can you give the full name?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: There were no Rankics in Sikiric, but rather, Dusan Prodanovic, is a person I forgot all about yesterday, but today I remember both his first and last name, and his house too was torched on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to finalise the house related to the name Kuca?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: As I said, the name of that man was Dusan Prodanovic, but he was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Sikiric then burned down that day except for those houses that I referred to as Muslim houses?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you repeat your question, Mr. Wubben, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Sikiric then burned down that day except from those houses that I referred to as Muslim houses?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can answer. Now, these houses were burning -- you noticed that these houses were burning at the time of the attack. Did you also notice houses burning in the area of your own family house, in Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it's convenient for you to stop here for the break, before you start something new, we'll stop here. If this is a short question, you may proceed. It's up to you, Mr. Wubben. I don't know what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I prefer to take up again this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we'll have a 25-minute break, then, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much more do you reckon you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Three-quarters of an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please try to restrict your questions to what is relevant to the indictment, because we've spent the past hour and a half dealing with matters which could have easily been dealt with in four or five questions, relevant only to the indictment, and the rest is not really important. I mean, I'm just opening your eyes. I'm being very patient, so is Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser, but we are missing the wood for the trees. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am going back now to where we left before the break, Witness, and I have a question to you: How did you notice that Sikiric, during the day of the attack, had been burned down? Did you saw after the burning of the houses? Did you visit the hamlet, or did you saw it from a distance or not?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: I was watching from a distance of about 300 metres from the village of Sikirici. That's where I was standing. So I could see the houses burning. I knew where the individual houses were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you continue, please? And what did you notice? Were there no flames anymore, and were the houses damaged or not?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes, damaged, torched. There was still smoke rising from there. There was nobody to put the smoke out. That would have been impossible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I would like to take you to the area of your own family house, because you were going in that direction. And did you also notice in that area that houses were burning on the day of the attack?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us the names of the families to whom those houses belonged to? I mean the names --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For example, is this important, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why is it important?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: It is important because she can, as living over there in that specific area, identify for Your Honours specific houses she can recall without showing me her a kind of photograph. It is a specific kind of identification and more specific when it comes to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you intend to prove, that those particular houses were burned or that only houses belonging to Serbs were burned down?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I want to prove both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Yes, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I just raise one matter, Your Honour, we have often in the English translation the word "torched" which might be taken to imply an act of human agency. I understand "palenja" the word in Bosnian can simply mean "burnt," provided it is understood that "torched" means nothing more than burnt, that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I'm taking it. Certainly not lit with a torch. I mean, it's -- definitely not. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please identify the names of the families, and, through that, the houses that were burning, as testified by you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: In my village, you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I mean in your village of Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Radovan's house was burning, but I can't remember his last name. If I can have a minute, please. Yes, Radoje Lukic and Radovan Lukic, these are two brothers. Miodrag Nikolic's house; Drago Nikolic's house; Besimir Stojanovic's house. These houses are next to Jovanovici, because the next village is the -- the next family is the Jovanovics, as I said. Petar's house was on fire on that day; this is something that I saw with my own eyes. Milo Jovanovic's house was burning. Milos Jovanovic's house; Milos was killed. Dzoko was killed too. Milo's wife -- mother, Zlata Jovanovic, too, was killed, and his daughter, Radenka Jovanovic. Milo's brother, Milan, was also killed on that day. Milos Jovanovic's house was burning, and he too was killed on the same day. Svetozar Jovanovic's house was burning too. Milenko's house too, that's the son, and the mother; it's a house they shared. Their field was burning too. Veseljka Jovanovic's house was burning and it burnt down, and she was wounded on that day but she survived. Miodrag Petrovic's house too was burning. That's even closer to my house. And another house was burning, but the owner was not in the area; he had been living in Sweden, and he still lives there. Stevo Filipovic's house was on fire. He died that day. Dragoljub Filipovic's house was burning. I saw flames rising from his house. Dragoljub was killed, as well as his son Dragan. And the house just in front of mine was burning too, at about 30 metres, Radovan Vucetic's house. He was also killed on that day. I saw him fall to the ground. I saw it with my own eyes. His son too was killed. His name was Milenko, and he was 17. Everything around my house was ablaze on that day, and they killed whoever they could. Should I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben, are you happy -- satisfied with the reply, or do you want more information?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: If she can identify more names of houses she saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can help her.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you saw also the house of Vucetic Cvetar burning?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Svetozar, yes, just across the away from our house. Further down the road, maybe 20 or 30 metres in front of my own house. Svetozar, yes, he too was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these were all houses burning during the attack in the area of where you lived?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- beside it, and then you don't have to be specific, also houses burning in Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: On that day, only Nikola Petrovic's house, I saw his house. But I've already told you about that. On that day, I didn't see anything else. It was getting dark and there was no time, so they withdrew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were these houses, as a consequence of that burning, were these damaged or burned down, or not?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Everyone had to build from scratch. Some walls needed repairing, everything that was necessary. That was the extent of the damage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you saw any of those houses you mentioned in Bjelovac being set on fire during the attack?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: All the houses that I've mentioned, I saw all of those. I know exactly where each of the houses were. I had been living in the area for so many years, and I'd never been away from the area --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, Witness, I have a question. Did you actually saw one of those houses, or more, being set on fire during the attack by someone, or not?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: I didn't see who set fire to the houses, but I saw smoke rising. I can't identify the persons who physically set fire to the houses. I wasn't near enough to see for myself. It just wasn't possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you notice when you get closer to your own family house?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Smoke. A house that was near my house, Bozo Todorovic's house, as I was trying to cut across, I passed near that house. It may have been at 3.00 or half past 3.00. Like I said, I saw flames rising from Dragoljub's house, from Stevo's house, there was smoke rising, Miodrag Petrovic's house, smoke coming out. I saw all the Jovanovic's houses, and there was smoke coming out of each and every one of those houses, thick smoke.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My next question is: What did you notice -- what did you saw when you came very close to your own house? Because you were getting in the direction of your own house, as you told us.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw bodies. I saw houses burning. When I reached Bozo Todorovic's house, the summer kitchen, I found him dead. I cried out to see whether there was anyone left alive. I think I stated that before. I saw another man whom I didn't know. He came out of a shed, a barn. He was wearing blue clothes with a backpack on his back, and a rifle in hand. He went behind the shed or the barn, and I was standing near Bozo's summer kitchen. I saw my husband at a corner of one of the other houses. I recognised his clothes. He wore a suit and a greyish jacket. There was a body there too, which I could not identify, but the next day, on the 15th, when I came over, I knew who the body belonged to. It was Milo Ilic's body. I started crying out near Bozo's house, Have you killed everyone? I screamed and I yelled. Something came flying and fell down near Bozo's house. It exploded. I didn't know what it was. I heard another man's voice from across the way from where I was standing, and he was shouting at me, Don't go there. It's not safe. I turned around, and it was Srecko Mihajlovic. He was standing near the ditch. I approached him, and I asked him what had happened to my family. He drew a deep sigh, and he replied, he said, All three of them have been killed. This was a heavy blow for me. I had to cope with the shock. I felt like I was about to die. I tried to pull myself together. I really don't know how something like that could have happened. I asked him how he knew that all of them had been killed, and he said Bogdana was off to look for her husband, because he had left and went to my house, but he couldn't get there because they killed him. She was there with the children and knew that they had been killed. This is a tragedy. Until 1996, I was not able to recover. I didn't realise that I was the only one left in this world. I couldn't pull myself back together. I didn't know where to go or what to do. Then I went back home in 1996, on the 18th of May, and my life finally went back to normal. I had been a refugee and I had not been able to go back home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: These were my questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Wubben. Madam Vidovic. Cross-examined by Ms. Vidovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Matic, can you please try to provide brief answers to my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And before we proceed, I would like to remind you, Madam Vidovic, and inform you, Madam Matic, that since you speak the same language, if you do not allow a small interval of time between question and answer, you will create a lot of confusion and a lot of difficulties for the interpreters. So my recommendation to you is to slow down and, between question and answer, allow a little bit of an interval. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Matic, today, at the beginning of your testimony, you told us that you were illiterate.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's sufficient. Thank you. In your earlier statement to the Prosecutor, you said that you had completed four years of primary school; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes, in 1956 or 1954. I can't be sure. I think it's 1954.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it not correct that at that time, as is the case today, children learned both scripts, Latin and Cyrillic, in the first grade of primary school?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's enough. Thank you. It is also correct that in the second grade of primary school, children learned to do sums and were instructed more broadly in our language, and in the third and fourth grade, they already wrote compositions.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes. But it's been a long time since then, many years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. Thank you. It is also correct that in the school system which prevailed when you were attending school, in the first four grades, in the third grade of primary school, children learned about certain writers, certain authors, such as Branko Copic, and had to read books by them as set reading.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true, but I've forgotten that, because I didn't renew that knowledge later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's correct, Mrs. Matic, is it not, that such things are not forgotten.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Well, that's happened in my case. I can read, I can read, but only block capitals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Matic. You also said that you were a housewife, but you also said that occasionally you worked at the school before the war. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: No. No, I was never employed. I never had a job. That might have been an error in interpretation. I was never employed anywhere. I was always a housewife.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Today, at one point during your testimony, when speaking of Mr. Berzadic, you said, I know him well, together he was a delegate with me in the local commune.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes, from time to time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it not true, Mrs. Matic, that when you were a delegate, you received various written materials so that you could inform the local population about them.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: No, never, never. I never received anything in writing. I was there on behalf of the women's anti-fascist club, and they kept me there only for the sake of my vote. And they only called upon me when there was some kind of meeting. But I never wrote anything or read anything there. That's the truth. When we had to vote for something, that's when they called upon me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mrs. Matic. I'll move on now to another topic. Before your testimony of today, the Prosecutor advised us that you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. had lost your reading glasses and the whole problem was solved when your glasses were found.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: I didn't lose them, I had forgotten them at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Matic, you are not illiterate, because otherwise you would not need the glasses, and you would have said so to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: I only use them to watch television. That's why I had the glasses made, so I could watch films on television. But I never managed to read the subtitles. There's not enough time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Vidovic, where do you plan to end on this, because --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Very soon, very soon, Your Honour, if you'll allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I don't see how it can change anything because she can, with a magnifying glass, read a couple of lines or a couple of sentences.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is not about the witness' glasses. Allow me to put a question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Prosecutor show you certain documents, referring to your previous testimony?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: You mean my statements?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How could you comment on those statements if you are unable to read them?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Because this other lady who was there read them out to me. It wasn't me who read them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Matic, you decided to say you were illiterate when you saw the documents we intended to show you; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I never decided to say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Matic. But in any case, you did say that you could read a few sentences that were typed.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Matic. Our documents are mostly written in such letters, so I will ask you to look at the documents anyway.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Well, this is going to be difficult. I see that you don't trust me, you don't believe me, but you should. I haven't come here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mrs. Matic, the ones who will decide what will happen is us three up here and not Ms. -- not Madam Vidovic. So if you have problems, just look at me and I will consult with the other two Judges and we will decide what to do. Yes, move ahead, please, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Matic, I will now ask you something else. Today you told us that tragically you lost your husband and two daughters in the war.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is also true that you yourself suffered certain consequences from shelling, and that you spent some time in a place near Vidakovica for recuperation.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I was gathering hay in my field. They were shooting, I don't know where from. This was before this attack. But I wasn't wounded, no, I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were never in hospital?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: No, not for that reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Matic. In your statement which you made in 2000, and I hope you'll recall it, you said that in Bjelovac there were only four Muslim houses.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes, four or five, but I think four, four families. After that they spread. But there were four families who were there. I can tell you there names --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will put the questions, so please just answer. Bjelovac had about 290 inhabitants; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you precisely. It's possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that in Bjelovac, in 1991, there were 59 Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: In Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, in Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: No. I can --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Matic, I will put the questions. Please allow me.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's correct, is it not, that in the very center of Bjelovac, several hundred metres away from your house, there were several Muslim families living there. Do the names of Sinanovic Rahman, Sead Nedzad mean anything to you? They had houses next to houses of Serb families, Ilic and Dzokanovic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Sead, yes, but not Nedzad at that time. He was not living there then. Not, it was only Sokla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sead and Rahman were?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were living there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Idud Basic Rifet [phoen] was a neighbour of yours, and he had a house in Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's close to the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Juso Efendic had an old house and a new house in the center of Bjelovac, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he did. Well, very well. Maybe --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please allow me, Mrs. Matic. Just a moment. It's also true, is it not, that Izet Osmanovic had a house near in the school in Bjelovac, and that in the very center there were also the houses of Alila Ajdar, Omer and Abid; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: They built houses there, but they didn't live there. They lived either in the same house, so it was one family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then there were seven houses belonging to the Efendic family, Muhamed Efendic and his brothers, and the house of Hajrudin Berzadic, whom you mentioned today which is very close to your house; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes. Berzadic, he lived there, yes. And as for the Efendics, those were only holiday homes. Jusuf Efendic's brother lived in Srebrenica. He had that house but he didn't live there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Also there were seven houses belonging to the Mujica --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down. The interpreter cannot catch the names.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: This was across the river. That was Zaluzje, that's on the other side from the river, because Bjelovac started at the river, on the riverbank, if you get my meaning. And across the river, yes, they were -- well, they weren't Muslims. How shall I put it? We called them Gypsies, but they weren't Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Matic, they were Muslims. Isn't it correct that the Mujanovic family of Nedza Faziariga [phoen] Mehmed and others, so on and so forth, isn't it true that Bjelovac, the center had 34 Muslim houses?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Those houses belonged to Zaluzje. The houses you are mentioning with in Zaluzje. They were not in my village. We were separated by a river, do you understand, a river. Bjelovac started from the -- Bjelovacka Rijeka to the Sikiricka Rijeka, those two rivers, and in between was my village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Matic, you will agree that in 1991 there was census?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a census, of course there was. But I don't -- it wasn't me who conducted the census.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would be very happy to show the precise data from the census, but I'm not sure that -- I will stop here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't need to, Madam Vidovic. You can just either suggest to her the exact figures and she will tell you whether she agrees or not. That's all. She doesn't need to see the document, unless you prefer to show the document to the Court, to the Trial Chamber, and to the Prosecution. That would suffice.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I certainly wouldn't stop you from tendering the document into evidence. But you don't need it show you to the witness. And may I again remind you both, you and the witness, Mrs. Matic, please, again, slow down and allow an interval between question and answer, because you are creating problems.
